lines.text: Sixty-six million years ago, on an evening like any other, a dinosaur lifted its head and looked up at the sky.
Somewhere up there, far too faint to see, a mountain of rock was falling toward the Earth. Nothing on the planet could have known it was coming.
Soon afterwards the dinosaurs were gone, along with about three-quarters of all the kinds of plants and animals on the planet.
Nobody was there to see it. Nobody wrote it down. And yet today we can say what happened, and where.
Its bones lie in museums today, still and silent. They can tell us what it looked like. They cannot tell us how its world ended.
This is the story of how we found out: from a line in the rock, a pinch of clay, a scratched grain of sand… and a report that nobody read.
For a long time, scientists argued. Had the climate slowly changed? Had disease spread? Had volcanoes poisoned the air?
None of these ideas could be tested. Was it a slow fade, or a sudden blow? The rocks did not seem to hold any answer.
Bones can tell you how big an animal was, and what it ate. But they cannot tell you how fast it died. For that, you need a clock.
Clue one: a line in the rock.
The geologist Walter Alvarez was studying the rock layers of a gorge near Gubbio, in Italy, reading the history of an ancient sea floor.
The rock there is like a book lying on its side. Each layer is a page, and every page is a slice of time.
Read from the bottom up, the stone book tells a story millions of years long. But which of its pages holds the ending?
In the older layers below, the stone is crowded with tiny fossils: the shells of plankton that once drifted in that sea in countless numbers.
Then comes a thin band of reddish clay, about a centimetre thick, no wider than a fingertip.
And above it, the tiny fossils are almost all gone. It is as if the story of life had paused. What could stop it so suddenly?
Walter realised what he was looking at. Whatever ended the age of the dinosaurs, it was written here, in a single centimetre of clay.
Walter wanted to know one simple thing. How long had that centimetre taken to form? A year? A thousand years?
Clue two: too much of a rare metal.
Walter took the question to his father, Luis Alvarez, a physicist who had won the Nobel Prize. Luis listened, and then he had an unusual idea.
Space dust falls on the Earth all the time, everywhere, in a slow and steady trickle.
That dust carries a rare metal called iridium. Measure how much of it is in the clay, and you can tell how long the clay took to settle. A little means quickly; a lot means a long time.
So they measured the clay, sample by sample, in a laboratory at Berkeley.
The answer made no sense. There was far too much iridium: dozens of times more than normal.
Not a slow trickle over thousands of years. Something had brought it all at once, from above.
It was as if a century of dust had fallen on a shelf in a single afternoon.
On the Earth's surface, iridium is rare. But some rocks that fall from space are rich in it.
In 1980, after checking and checking again, the Alvarez team published their answer: an asteroid about ten kilometres across had struck the Earth.
Ten kilometres across: a mountain of rock, taller than Mount Everest, falling out of the sky.
Clue three: scars in the sand.
Many scientists did not believe it. A rock from space, wiping out the dinosaurs? If an asteroid had really hit, the evidence should be everywhere.
And it was. The same iridium-rich layer turned up in rocks around the world.
Under the microscope, that layer held grains of quartz crossed by fine straight lines, like scratches on glass.
Quartz is one of the toughest minerals on Earth. Ordinary forces barely mark it. Only a tremendous shock can.
This shocked quartz forms only under enormous pressure, the kind made by an impact.
Every grain was a witness to the blow. But where had it landed? Where was the crater?
Clue four: a ring under the jungle.
A crater that size should be enormous. Scientists searched the oceans and deserts of the world, looking for a scar. Something that big should have been easy to spot. Yet nobody could find it.
But it had already been found, years earlier, by people who were not looking for dinosaurs at all.
In 1978, Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo were geophysicists for Mexico's national oil company. They were surveying the Yucatán coast for oil, with instruments that sense the hidden rocks below.
They were looking for oil, deep beneath the jungle. Instead, they found something far older and far stranger.
Their instruments drew a strange shape: half of a giant ring, buried deep beneath the ground.
The other half lay under the sea. Together they made a circle far too big to notice from the surface.
In 1981 they presented it at a scientific meeting. Almost nobody noticed.
The report went back on the shelf. Dust settled on it, while the rest of the world kept searching.
Then, in 1990, a young scientist named Alan Hildebrand followed the trail of clues all the way to the Yucatán.
He tracked down old drill cores that the oil company had pulled up from deep inside the ring years before, and stored away.
And inside that rock? Shocked minerals, carrying exactly the same scars as the grains found all around the world.
In 1991 the crater got its name, from a small village near its centre: Chicxulub.
The ring is about one hundred and eighty kilometres wide: big enough to swallow a whole city and the countryside around it.
So here is the twist. The crater had been found more than a decade before it got its name, and filed away in a company report.
The smoking gun was not hidden in the rock. It was hidden on a shelf.
So, after all those clues, what killed the dinosaurs?
An asteroid about ten kilometres across struck the coast of what is now Mexico, sixty-six million years ago.
The blast left a crater about one hundred and eighty kilometres wide, now buried beneath the jungle and the sea.
The impact threw dust and molten rock high into the sky, laid the iridium layer around the planet, and scarred grains of sand on the way down.
Darkness and cold followed. With little sunlight, plants withered, and the food chains that the giants depended on collapsed.
But not everything died.
Small mammals, hiding in burrows, survived. Their descendants would one day become us.
And some dinosaurs survived too. We call them birds.
Every sparrow and every eagle is a living dinosaur, a survivor of that day.
Think about it. Everything we know about that day came from a centimetre of clay, a metal from space, a scratched grain of sand… and a forgotten report.
And it began with a simple question from a father and son: how long does a centimetre of clay take to form?
So the next time you hear a bird at dawn, remember: it is the last of the dinosaurs, flying out of the longest night on Earth.
